name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BODY_FLUIDS_AND_CIRCULATION_SEQUENCING_Q01 - Chronological sequence of blood coagulation cascade events

questiontext.text:
Arrange the following biochemical and cellular events occurring during the mechanism of blood coagulation in the correct chronological sequence following tissue trauma or vascular injury:

(I) Conversion of inactive prothrombin into active thrombin by an enzyme complex in the presence of calcium ions.

(II) Formation of the enzyme complex thrombokinase through a cascade of linked enzymatic reactions.

(III) Stimulation of platelets and damaged tissues to release factors that initiate the coagulation mechanism.

(IV) Entanglement of dead and damaged formed elements within a network of threads to form a dark reddish-brown clot.

(V) Cleavage of soluble fibrinogen into insoluble fibrin threads by thrombin.

Which of the following represents the correct sequential order of these events?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Initiation by Platelets and Damaged Tissue
Physical injury stimulates platelets and damaged vascular endothelium to release thromboplastic factors that trigger the clotting mechanism.

Step 2: Generation of the Thrombokinase Complex
These released factors activate a cascade process involving inactive plasma factors in a series of linked enzymic reactions, leading to the formation of the enzyme complex thrombokinase.

Step 3: Conversion of Prothrombin to Thrombin
In the presence of calcium ions, thrombokinase catalyses the conversion of the inactive plasma protein prothrombin into the active proteolytic enzyme thrombin.

Step 4: Formation of Insoluble Fibrin Threads
Thrombin acts enzymatically upon soluble fibrinogen in plasma, polymerising it into long insoluble threads of fibrin.

Step 5: Formation of the Coagulum
The insoluble fibrin threads create an intricate meshwork that traps erythrocytes, leukocytes, and damaged cellular debris, forming the definitive clot or coagulum that seals the wound.

Final Answer: The correct chronological sequence is release of initiation factors by platelets and injured tissue, followed by enzymatic formation of thrombokinase, conversion of prothrombin to active thrombin, conversion of fibrinogen into fibrin threads, and trapping of formed elements to form the clot.

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_BODY_FLUIDS_AND_CIRCULATION_SEQUENCING_Q02 - Sequence of cardiac excitation and ventricular ejection

questiontext.text:
The following events take place during the transmission of cardiac excitation and the subsequent ventricular pumping phase of a human cardiac cycle:

(I) Transmission of the electrical impulse down the inter-ventricular septum along the bundle of His and spreading through the Purkinje fibres.

(II) Generation of an action potential by the sino-atrial node in the upper right wall of the right atrium.

(III) Sharp rise in ventricular pressure forcing open the semilunar valves to eject blood into the pulmonary artery and aorta.

(IV) Arrival and conduction of the action potential through the atrio-ventricular node.

(V) Onset of ventricular systole increasing intraventricular pressure and causing closure of the atrio-ventricular valves.

Which of the following represents the correct logical sequence of these events?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Initiation of Electrical Impulse at the Sino-Atrial Node
The sino-atrial node located in the right upper corner of the right atrium possesses the highest rate of autoexcitability (70 to 75 action potentials per minute). It initiates the cardiac cycle by generating an action potential that spreads across the atrial musculature, triggering atrial systole.

Step 2: Conduction to the Atrio-Ventricular Node
From the atria, the wave of depolarisation reaches the atrio-ventricular node situated in the lower left corner of the right atrium close to the atrio-ventricular septum, where it is briefly delayed before conducting toward the ventricles.

Step 3: Propagation Through the Bundle of His and Purkinje Fibres
The action potential enters the atrio-ventricular bundle (bundle of His) traversing the inter-ventricular septum, splitting into right and left bundle branches that distribute minute Purkinje fibres throughout the ventricular myocardium.

Step 4: Ventricular Contraction and Closure of Atrio-Ventricular Valves
The coordinated excitation of ventricular muscle fibres initiates ventricular systole. The immediate increase in intraventricular pressure forces blood toward the atria, which promptly closes the tricuspid and bicuspid (mitral) valves to prevent backflow, generating the first heart sound.

Step 5: Opening of Semilunar Valves and Ventricular Ejection
As ventricular myocardial contraction continues, intraventricular pressure surpasses the pressure within the major outflow tracts, forcing the semilunar valves of the pulmonary artery and systemic aorta open to eject blood into the circulation.

Final Answer: The correct chronological order is impulse initiation at the sino-atrial node, conduction through the atrio-ventricular node, transmission down the bundle of His and Purkinje fibres, closure of atrio-ventricular valves during early ventricular systole, and opening of semilunar valves for ventricular ejection.
